title: Burrata, pomodoro e basilico
subtitle: Burrata with heritage tomatoes and basil
excerpt: Whole burrata served with sliced ripe heritage tomatoes, torn basil, flaky salt, and excellent olive oil. The simplest and best Italian antipasto when tomatoes are at their peak.
sourceNotes: The pairing of fresh cheese, ripe tomatoes, and basil is a fundamental of southern Italian cooking and appears in the same tradition as caprese. Burrata pomodoro e basilico is a contemporary extension of this tradition documented in Pugliese and Neapolitan restaurant cooking from the 1990s onwards. It appears in Giorgio Locatelli's Made in Italy (2006) and in multiple Italian antipasto references.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cannot be made ahead. Slice the tomatoes and assemble at the last minute.

content.text: This is a dish that only exists in August. Outside peak tomato season, the tomatoes will not have enough flavour to carry their share of the plate, and the result will be disappointing regardless of how good the burrata is. If you can find heritage or vine tomatoes that have been grown outside and are soft enough to smell from a metre away, this is one of the best things on a summer table. If the tomatoes are pale and odourless from a supermarket cold store, make something else.

items.prepNote: bought on the day they are made
heritage or vine tomatoes, mixed varieties if possible, at room temperature

content.text: Slice the tomatoes into thick rounds or halves depending on their size. Arrange them on a large plate or platter, slightly overlapping. Season the tomatoes generously with sea salt flakes and a little black pepper.
Pat the burrata dry. Place the burrata in the centre of the plate or at one side of the tomatoes. Score the top with a small cross if you want the cream to flow at the table.
Tear the basil leaves and scatter them over everything. Drizzle the olive oil generously over the tomatoes and over the burrata. Serve immediately with grilled or fresh bread.

items.symptom: Tomatoes are watery and tasteless on the plate
items.cause: Salted too far in advance, or tomatoes of poor quality
items.fix: Salt the tomatoes just before serving. There is no fixing poor-quality tomatoes: do not make this dish when tomatoes are out of season.

items.symptom: Olive oil tastes bitter and harsh
items.cause: Too-assertive olive oil, or poor quality
items.fix: Use a balanced, fruity olive oil from Puglia or Sicily rather than an aggressively peppery Tuscan variety. Taste the oil on bread before using it.

content.text: This is summer food from the mezzogiorno: Puglia, Campania, and Sicily. These are the regions where both the tomato and the cheese traditions are strongest. The pairing of burrata with tomatoes and basil is a close relation of the caprese. The running cream of the burrata adds a richness that mozzarella cannot match. It appears on the terrace menus of Italian agriturismi in August and at the outdoor tables of Italian restaurants worldwide. It is the dish chefs put on menus when they want to show they understand good ingredients.
